clue.text: Overly snazzy dresser — male, female in hi-vis coat, possibly

indicators.note: 'possibly' says the letters could become something else, one possible rearrangement among many

parts.note: M is the standard abbreviation for male
F is the standard abbreviation for female
taken as written
taken as written, hyphen dropped

explanation.surface: A man or woman parading about in a high-visibility jacket is mocked as a dandy who dresses far too loudly.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole run from 'male' to 'coat' is raw material: M and F from the abbreviations plus every letter of IN HI-VIS COAT, thirteen in all.
explanation.definitionFit: A fashion victim slavishly follows trends, however ridiculous, so the term suits someone whose clothes are far too flashy.

clue.text: Entirely available in every country?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an idiom for completely or in every respect
second meaning, read literally: a product meant for every nation on the globe; the question mark flags the playful reading

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one sentence about global availability, but 'Entirely' stands alone as the idiomatic sense, and the rest is the phrase taken word by word.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom expresses exactness or completeness, and literally the phrase describes something provided to every nation on earth.

clue.text: Engaging source of some help about parking

indicators.note: the source of a word is where it starts, so only its opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of 'some'

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: aid is help
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: Someone describes an attractive source of a little help with parking.
explanation.walkthrough: S, then AID wrapped around P. SAPID is a rare word, literally 'flavourful', and by extension interesting or engaging.
explanation.definitionFit: Sapid means savoury and, figuratively, agreeable or interesting to the mind, the same sense as engaging.

clue.text: Gut feeling about day one is ill-defined

indicators.note: 'about' means surrounding, so one piece wraps around the others

parts.note: a gut feeling is an instinct
D is the abbreviation for day
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A hunch about the first day turns out to be vague.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Day one' looks like a start date, but it is two separate abbreviations, D and I, which go inside INSTINCT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something indistinct lacks clear outlines or sharpness, which is what ill-defined describes.

clue.text: Negative response is bad sign, mostly unpleasant

indicators.note: 'mostly' means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: the negative reply
taken as written
an omen is a bad sign, here losing its final letter

explanation.surface: Being turned down is a bad omen, and mostly an unpleasant one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' looks like a link word but is part of the answer; OMEN loses its N.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisome means offensive or disgusting, especially of smells, so it is a stronger synonym for unpleasant.

clue.text: European amongst family probing documents in European country

indicators.note: to be amongst others is to sit inside the group, so one letter goes within
a probe goes into something, so this piece is pushed inside another

parts.note: ID means identity documents
a clan is a family group
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A European official within a family is investigating paperwork somewhere in Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter goes in after the family's first letter, not at its centre, and then the whole lot sits between the two letters of the documents.
explanation.definitionFit: Iceland is the North Atlantic island nation, a sovereign state of Europe, so it is an example of the category.

clue.text: Slip in smutty poem?

indicators.note: 'in' says the wanted letters sit inside the following words

parts.note: the letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A careless moment within a rude bit of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the end of 'smutty' and the start of 'poem'; the question mark admits the surface is a bit cheeky.
explanation.definitionFit: A slip is a small mistake, and a typo is a small error made when typing or printing text.

clue.text: Mike is name to use roughly

parts.note: Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written
a handle is slang for a name or nickname

explanation.surface: Mike is the nickname given to someone known for handling things roughly.
explanation.walkthrough: A handle as a name is the CB-radio sense, a user's chosen call name, which the surface disguises as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To mishandle something is to treat it carelessly or clumsily, which matches using it roughly.

clue.text: Best prevent gambler's conviction? Not entirely

indicators.note: something not entirely present is incomplete, so the final letter is lost

parts.note: to get a defendant off is to secure an acquittal, and a 'better' is one who bets

explanation.surface: Someone tries hard to stop a gambler being convicted, but only half succeeds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' is read as a punter (more usually spelt bettor). Getting him off a charge is GET THE BETTER OFF, and dropping the last F leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, best means to defeat or outdo someone, which is the meaning of the idiom.

clue.text: Charge, one very serious, involving force asking questions urgently?

indicators.note: to involve is to include within, so one letter is taken inside

parts.note: a rap is a criminal charge, as in 'take the rap'
I is the Roman numeral for one
dire means extremely serious
F is the symbol for force in physics

explanation.surface: A grave accusation is made, and a police force is brought in to interrogate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Force' looks like the police but is just F, placed inside DIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapid-fire questioning comes in quick succession, so the adjective describes questions asked hurriedly; the question mark flags the loose fit.

clue.text: I'm abandoning hobby making imitation jewellery

indicators.note: to abandon is to leave behind, so those letters go missing

parts.note: a pastime is a hobby
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone gives up a hobby of crafting fake jewels.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the I and M out of PASTIME to leave the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Paste is a hard glassy compound used to make imitation gems, and costume jewellery made from it.

clue.text: Rotation of Earth limiting depth in swimming pools

indicators.note: a rotation turns something round, so the letters run backwards
to limit is to set bounds, so the outer piece encloses another

parts.note: earth is soil
D is the abbreviation for depth

explanation.surface: The spinning of the planet supposedly limits how deep swimming pools can be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rotation of Earth' sounds like the planet spinning, but earth here is soil, turned around to LIOS before D goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: A lido is a public open-air swimming pool, so the plural is a collection of outdoor pools.

clue.text: Old can getting twisted: it's round, but not circular

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old

indicators.note: twisting something round turns it the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: can is slang for a toilet, as is lav

explanation.surface: An old tin can gets crushed and bent so that it is round but no longer a true circle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' is not a tin but the slang for a toilet; lav is the British short form of lavatory.
explanation.definitionFit: An oval is a rounded shape that is elongated rather than a perfect circle, exactly the distinction the definition draws.

clue.text: Charlie invested in profitable piece of information

indicators.note: money invested in something is put inside it, so one letter goes within

parts.note: fat can mean lucrative, as in a fat profit or a fat contract
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Charlie has put money into a lucrative tip-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invested' and 'profitable' paint a financial scene, but the investment is just C going into FAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A fact is a single item of true knowledge or data, so it counts as a piece of information.

clue.text: Indicator of hills? Crampon out, active

indicators.note: active letters are lively and moving about, so they change places

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A climber packs away the spiked crampon and gets moving up the hills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' looks like the anagram signal, but it is part of the fodder; 'active' does the stirring.
explanation.definitionFit: A contour map shows elevation with lines joining points of equal height, so it reveals where hills rise.

clue.text: Source of lamb in exotic stew is something of a joke

indicators.note: 'in' places one piece within another

parts.note: a tagine is a North African slow-cooked stew

indicators.note: the source of a word is where it starts, so only its opening letter counts

parts.note: the first letter of 'lamb'

explanation.surface: Finding where the lamb came from in a foreign stew turns out to be a bit of a laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: Lamb is a classic tagine ingredient, which helps hide that only its L is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: A tagline is the punchline of a joke or a catchy slogan, so it is a part of a joke.

clue.text: Gossip about translation of Proust in classy eatery

indicators.note: 'about' means surrounding, so the outer piece wraps another

parts.note: gab is idle chatter

indicators.note: a translation renders words in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Diners chatter about a new translation of Proust over dinner in a smart restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: GAB opens to take the jumbled letters of the French novelist's name. A gastropub is a British pub serving restaurant-quality food.
explanation.definitionFit: A gastropub is a pub known for high-quality cooking, so it is an upmarket place to eat.

clue.text: Reckless opportunity that is securing diamonds

indicators.note: to secure is to hold fast, so the outer piece grips another inside

parts.note: a door is an opening or opportunity, as in 'opens doors'
i.e. abbreviates id est, that is
D is the card-game abbreviation for diamonds

explanation.surface: A rash chance to grab some diamonds, like a heist.
explanation.walkthrough: Here 'securing' means holding between, so the opportunity and the 'that is' abbreviation together clamp the diamonds in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A do-or-die attempt risks everything with no thought of retreat, so it is desperate and reckless.

clue.text: Cuts out former heretical groups?

parts.note: ex- means former
a sect is a group breaking from orthodox belief

explanation.surface: Religious splinter groups of old are being excluded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cuts out' sounds like 'excludes', but it is the surgical verb; EX and SECTS simply join.
explanation.definitionFit: To exsect is a surgical term meaning to remove by cutting, so exsects means removes by excision.

clue.text: Verse criticism supported by that chap

indicators.note: in a down entry, something supported has its support beneath it, so the later piece comes second

parts.note: a strop is an angry outburst, here taken as a telling-off
he refers to that man

explanation.surface: Some critical words about a poem are backed by a particular man.
explanation.walkthrough: A strop is really a fit of bad temper, so taking it as criticism is a stretch; the verse sense of the answer comes from Greek drama.
explanation.definitionFit: A strophe is a stanza or section of a Greek choral ode, so it is a unit of verse.

clue.text: In front of detective, whips gem

indicators.note: being in front means coming earlier in the line, so the next piece leads

parts.note: a cat (cat-o'-nine-tails) is a whip
a private eye is a detective

explanation.surface: Standing before an investigator, someone produces a precious stone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In front of detective' places the whips first. 'Whips' looks like a verb, as if someone snatches the gem.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat's-eye is a gemstone, such as chrysoberyl, whose light band resembles the slit pupil of a cat.

clue.text: See you applaud international orchestra at the outset

parts.note: to cheer is to applaud
I is the abbreviation for international

indicators.note: the outset is the very beginning, so just the opening letter is used

parts.note: the first letter of 'orchestra'

explanation.surface: A concertgoer applauds a visiting world orchestra as the performance begins.
explanation.walkthrough: CHEER, I, O in order. Cheerio is a British informal goodbye.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are casual farewells said when parting company, so the British goodbye matches 'see you'.

clue.text: Lady's fingers are almost withdrawn after one kiss initially

indicators.note: 'almost' means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped
'after' places the earlier piece behind what follows it in the clue
'initially' means at the start, so the opening letters are taken

parts.note: the first letters of 'one' and 'kiss'

indicators.note: something withdrawn is drawn back, so the letters go the other way

parts.note: taken as written, losing its final letter

explanation.surface: A woman's hands are nearly pulled away after a single kiss at the start of a romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lady's fingers' looks like the woman's hand, but it is the vegetable's other name. ARE loses its E and turns round, then follows OK.
explanation.definitionFit: Okra is the green pod vegetable also called ladies' fingers, from its long slender tapering shape.

clue.text: Couple shunning cold Scottish hillside

indicators.note: to shun is to keep away from, so that letter is left out

parts.note: a brace is a pair, used especially of game birds
C is the tap abbreviation for cold

explanation.surface: Two people avoid a chilly slope in the Highlands.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove C from BRACE.
explanation.definitionFit: Brae is the Scots word for a steep bank or hill slope, as in many Scottish place names.

clue.text: University linked computers — about 1,000? Not satisfied

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for university

indicators.note: 'about' means surrounding, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: a net or network is a set of linked computers
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: A university's network of about a thousand machines still falls short of demand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about 1,000' reads as roughly a thousand, but 'about' is the container signal around M.
explanation.definitionFit: Unmet is used of needs, demands or conditions that have not been fulfilled, the same as not satisfied.

clue.text: Message for family seat turned up, with start missing

indicators.note: a missing start means the opening letter is gone
in a down entry, turning something up makes it read from bottom to top

parts.note: the seat is the bottom, losing its first letter

explanation.surface: A note left at the family's country seat has been dug up but its opening words are lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Family seat' suggests a stately home, but 'seat' alone is the backside, BOTTOM.
explanation.definitionFit: A family motto is a short maxim on a coat of arms expressing the household's guiding principle.

clue.text: Pop group reduced promotional material

indicators.note: something reduced is cut short, so the last letter is lost

parts.note: a blurb is promotional text, as on a book jacket

explanation.surface: A band's publicity has been trimmed back.
explanation.walkthrough: BLURB loses its final B. Blur is a British band famous in the 1990s Britpop era.
explanation.definitionFit: Blur, fronted by Damon Albarn, is an English rock band, so it is an example of a pop group.

clue.text: Error when cutting second large part of jacket

indicators.note: cutting removes something, so a letter is taken out

parts.note: a lapse is an error
S is the abbreviation for second
L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A tailor's slip while cutting a second, large section of a jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: The tailoring scene makes 'cutting' sound literal; it means S is removed from LAPSE, then L is added.
explanation.definitionFit: A lapel is the folded flap on the front of a jacket below the collar, so it is a component of the garment.

clue.text: Border difficulties recalled in safe surroundings

indicators.note: 'in' places one piece inside another
surroundings enclose, so the outer piece goes all the way round

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe

indicators.note: something recalled is called back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a mire is a difficult situation

explanation.surface: Problems at the frontier are remembered from the safety of home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Safe' reads as an adjective but is the noun, a strongbox; peter for a safe is old British underworld slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A perimeter is the boundary line enclosing an area, so it is the outer border of a space.

clue.text: Academic's trouble accepting ordinary legal notion

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so one letter goes inside

parts.note: a burden is a trouble or load
the possessive turned round: X's burden is the burden of X
prof is short for professor
O is the abbreviation for ordinary, as in O level

explanation.surface: A professor's difficulties involve some everyday legal idea.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive is read backwards, so 'the academic's trouble' becomes 'the trouble of the academic', with the ordinary letter tucked inside the professor.
explanation.definitionFit: In law the burden of proof is the obligation on one party to establish the facts, a core principle of trials.
